chunks.content: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY One key strength of our study is its multicentre phase 1b/2 design, which incorporates both a dose-escalation phase and an expansion cohort. In this study, a novel first-line combinatorial therapy regimen for advanced gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction cancer was established, integrating fruquintinib, sintilimab and the oxaliplatin+capecitabine regimen. The study design has several limitations, primarily the loss of research equipoise due to its open-label nature, as well as potential biases and interpretational challenges inherent in single-arm study designs. Introduction According to GLOBOCAN 2022, gastric cancer (GC) accounted for approximately 4.9% of all new cancer cases and 6.8% of all cancer deaths globally. The incidence and mortality rates represent nearly half of the global population, highlighting a concerning situation regarding the prevention and control efforts. In China, GC ranks as the third most prevalent malignant tumour in terms of both incidence and mortality. Of the 1.089 million new cases of GC reported worldwide, about 43.9% cases and approximately 49% of deaths due to GC occur in China. 2 Advanced GC is difficult to be surgically resected and its prognosis is poor. Treatment options for unresectable GC include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy and palliative therapy depending on the development of the tumour. Chemotherapeutic regimens for gastric/gastro-oesophageal junction (G/GEJ) cancer primarily consist of fluorouracil (antimetabolite), platinum and paclitaxel, often in various combinations. The median overall survival (OS) of patients who benefited from the standard first-line (1L) chemotherapy ranges from 10 months to 14 months. In this regard, combinatorial treatment options using immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) monoclonal antibodies have shown promising outcomes. At present, targeted anti-programmed cell death 1 protein (anti-PD-1) monoclonal antibodies such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for use in GC. Currently, PD-1 inhibitors in combination with chemotherapy have been approved as the 1L treatment for advanced GC. In the ATTRACTION-4 trial, patients with advanced GC received nivolumab plus chemotherapy or placebo plus chemotherapy as the 1L treatment. The objective response rate (ORR) in the nivolumab plus chemotherapy group was 57.5%. In the CheckMate 649 study, chemotherapy combined with nivolumab significantly prolonged the survival with higher ORR versus chemotherapy alone in the full set, as well as the subset with CPS (Combined Positive Score, CPS)≥1 and CPS≥5. Among all randomised patients, the ORR of nivolumab plus chemotherapy was 59%. On the basis of results from the ORIENT-16 study, sintilimab, a selective anti-PD-1 antibody, combined with the XELOX regimen (the oxaliplatin plus capecitabine chemotherapy regimen) was approved as the 1L treatment for advanced GC in China, and this indication was also included in the Chinese national health insurance system in 2023. Studies have also suggested that immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy has a certain value in Asian patients with GC, but the efficacy is not satisfactory and further research is warranted. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) and Japanese guidelines recommend zolbetuximab (Vyloy) combination therapy as 1L treatment for CLDN18.2-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2 overexpression negative, unresectable advanced or recurrent GC, based on phase 3 SPOTLIGHT and GLOW trial data. In these trials, zolbetuximab plus mFOLFOX6 (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin) prolonged median progression-free survival (mPFS) and OS to 10.61 months and 18.23 months, whereas zolbetuximab plus CAPOX (capecitabine, oxaliplatin) achieved 8.21 months and 14.39 months. Following the approval of Zolbetuximab for marketing in China in December 2024, the 2025 Chinese guidelines recommend Zolbetuximab as 1L therapy for Claudin18.2-positive, HER2-negative locally advanced and unresectable or metastatic gastric and GEJ adenocarcinoma. From a mechanistic standpoint, successful immunotherapy requires not just the infiltration of immune cells, but also an immune-supportive microenvironment that fosters the proliferation and functionality of T cells. The precise mechanism of the anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)/anti-Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) interaction is likely multifactorial, but it is tempting to speculate that antivascular effects of VEGF inhibition, especially in combination with cytotoxic agents, may result in release of tumour antigens, thus facilitating immunotherapy. The additive or synergistic effects of combining VEGF inhibitors with cytotoxic agents may be partly attributed to the direct anti-vascular actions of cytotoxic agents, which potentiate the pro-apoptotic effects of anti-VEGF agents on vascular endothelial cells. Some studies have provided another hypothesis that using anti-angiogenic drugs can lead to normalised blood vessels, result in pruning of endothelial cells not covered by pericytes and a reduction in the tortuosity and hyperpermeability of tumour vessels, and these effects are expected to reduce tumour interstitial pressure and lead to enhanced uptake of cytotoxic agents and antibodies by the tumour. Fruquintinib, a highly selective small molecule inhibitor of VEGF receptor (VEGFR) specifically targets the VEGFR kinase family (VEGFR1, VEGFR2 and VEGFR3), was approved in September 2018 for third-line treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (CRC) in patients who had received prior fluorouracil-based, oxaliplatin-based and irinotecan-based chemotherapy and were resistant

anti-angiogenic drugs can lead to normalised blood vessels, result in pruning of endothelial cells not covered by pericytes and a reduction in the tortuosity and hyperpermeability of tumour vessels, and these effects are expected to reduce tumour interstitial pressure and lead to enhanced uptake of cytotoxic agents and antibodies by the tumour. Fruquintinib, a highly selective small molecule inhibitor of VEGF receptor (VEGFR) specifically targets the VEGFR kinase family (VEGFR1, VEGFR2 and VEGFR3), was approved in September 2018 for third-line treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (CRC) in patients who had received prior fluorouracil-based, oxaliplatin-based and irinotecan-based chemotherapy and were resistant or ineligible for VEGF/VEGFR-targeted therapy. In December 2024, fruquintinib in combination with sintilimab received conditional approval for advanced mismatch repair-proficient endometrial cancer patients who had failed prior systemic anticancer therapy and were ineligible for radical surgery or radiotherapy. In June 2025, the New Drug Application for fruquintinib in combination with sintilimab in patients with locally advanced or metastatic renal cell carcinoma who had failed prior treatment with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor was accepted for review by the NMPA (National Medical Products Administration) of China. Currently, combination regimens of fruquintinib with chemotherapy or immunotherapy are being further investigated in multiple solid tumours, including GC, colorectal cancer, cervical cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma. Several preclinical studies suggest a significant shift in the treatment approach of GC, emphasising the combination of antivascular therapy and immunotherapy. The SPACE trial demonstrated encouraging outcomes of camrelizumab plus apatinib and chemotherapy as a 1L treatment for advanced GC. The mPFS was reported to be 8.4 months, ORR 76.5%, while the disease control rate (DCR) reached 91.2%. Furthermore, the TALENT trial, a single-arm multicentric study, investigated the combination of tislelizumab, anlotinib and oxaliplatin+capecitabine (CAPEOX) as a 1L treatment for unresectable, advanced or metastatic G/GEJ cancer. The interim analysis of the initial 38 cases indicated an ORR of 75.86% with manageable toxicity, thereby increasing the confidence in this combination therapy. It is proposed that incorporating fruquintinib with chemotherapy, in conjunction with immunotherapy, could have the potential to modulate the immune microenvironment. This combination has the potential to transit the tumour microenvironment from an immunosuppressive phase to the one that supports immune activity. Furthermore, chemotherapy-induced tumour cell death may enhance immunogenicity and may work synergistically with ICIs, thereby potentially enhancing both short-term and long-term treatment outcomes for patients with advanced G/GEJ cancer. Two studies aiming to investigate the safety and efficacy of fruquintinib combined with sintilimab and chemotherapy for the treatment of advanced G/GEJ cancer have been sequentially initiated. In a single-arm, phase 2 trial, fruquintinib in combination with sintilimab and SOX (S-1 and oxaliplatin) is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fruquintinib plus SOX as conversion therapy for initially unresectable G/GEJ adenocarcinoma who have not received prior antitumour therapy, and the preliminary results showed an acceptable toxicity and induced very high R0 resection (100%), pathological complete response (CR) (11.1%) and downstaging rate (72.2%) in patients with primary unresectable GC/GEJC. However, limited evidence supports the use of fruquintinib combined with sintilimab and CAPEOX regimen in treatment of unresectable advanced, refractory or metastatic G/GEJ cancer. This FUNCTION trial will address this gap to assess the clinical efficacy and safety of this combinatorial treatment for G/GEJ cancers, providing critical evidence for optimal and effective treatment of these patients. Methods and analysis Study design FUNCTION study ( NCT06329973 ) is a phase Ib/II, multicentre, single-arm, prospective, open-label clinical study, designed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of fruquintinib, sintilimab and the CAPEOX regimen as a 1L combinatorial therapy for advanced G/GEJ cancer. This study will initiate with a dose-escalating phase for identifying the optimum combinatorial dose of fruquintinib (ie, from three dose groups, namely 3 mg, 4 mg and 5 mg per oral. d1–14, with three patients in each group (n=3)) followed by a dose expansion phase for determining the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). The study design is outlined in . Treatment All patients will undergo a screening period (up to 28 days) followed by a treatment period (until the investigator determines that the study drug is no longer used), safety follow-up (after the administration of last dose of the study drug or before the start of new anticancer treatment, whichever occurs first) and survival follow-up (until death, loss to follow-up, withdrawal of consent or termination of the study). The study flowchart is detailed in the . The dose-escalating phase of this study will use a 3+3 design, incorporating an escalating oral daily dosage of fruquintinib ranging from statistics 3–5 mg (increasing 1 mg per level) fruquintinib for days 1–14. This will be combined with intravenous administration of sintilimab 200 mg on day 1, capecitabine at 800 mg/m 2 , taken orally twice daily for days 1–14 and one-time intravenous dose of oxaliplatin at 130 mg/m 2 , on day 1,

occurs first) and survival follow-up (until death, loss to follow-up, withdrawal of consent or termination of the study). The study flowchart is detailed in the . The dose-escalating phase of this study will use a 3+3 design, incorporating an escalating oral daily dosage of fruquintinib ranging from statistics 3–5 mg (increasing 1 mg per level) fruquintinib for days 1–14. This will be combined with intravenous administration of sintilimab 200 mg on day 1, capecitabine at 800 mg/m 2 , taken orally twice daily for days 1–14 and one-time intravenous dose of oxaliplatin at 130 mg/m 2 , on day 1, within a 21-day cycle. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and RP2D of fruquintinib with a dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) assessment will be determined in the phase 1b study period of the first cycle. DLTs were defined as any of the following toxicities occurring during the DLT period that are deemed to be related to study treatment: grade ≥4 haematological toxicities, grade ≥3 non-haematological toxicities and any toxicities necessitating discontinuation of fruquintinib or sintilimab for 21 days or more. The RP2D is defined as the optimal therapeutic dose at or below the MTD. If the study does not reach an MTD, 5 mg will be designated as the MTD. The RP2D of fruquintinib will be used in the subsequent dose expansion phase. Following 6–8 cycles, as judged by the investigator, fruquintinib in combination with sintilimab will be administered as maintenance therapy. Patients likely to undergo radical resection after treatment or those who can achieve a disease-free state via a combination of surgery and radiofrequency are eligible for various interventions, including surgery, radiofrequency, microwave, radiotherapy or other localised treatment options aimed at achieving a disease-free state. Fruquintinib should be discontinued one cycle prior to surgery. On achieving a disease-free state, sintilimab combined with chemotherapy is recommended as the adjuvant treatment (oxaliplatin up to eight cycles). Study population and recruitment A total of 70 eligible patients with HER2 negative/unknown status G/GEJ cancer will be enrolled from 16 hospitals in China based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The study is planned to be conducted at 16 public hospitals. To date, eight centres have obtained ethical approval and commenced patient recruitment, including the Affiliated Cancer Hospital of Zhengzhou University & Henan Cancer Hospital, Luohe Central Hospital, The First People’s Hospital of Shangqiu, Luoyang Central Hospital and Luoyang Central Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou University, Xinyang Central Hospital, Jiangsu Province Hospital and The First Affiliated Hospital with Nanjing Medical University and Jiangsu Women and Children Health Hospital, Longgang District People’s Hospital of Shenzhen and The Second Affiliated Hospital, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shanxi Cancer Hospital. Hunan Cancer Hospital and The Affiliated Cancer Hospital of Xiangya School of Medicine, Central South University, and Mengjin People’s Hospital of Luoyang are in the process of preparing ethical documentation and six centres are pending activation. Six public hospitals remain pending initiation. Participant enrolment, initiated on 28 February 024, is ongoing, with 38 participants enrolled to date (see for further details). The planned primary completion date is 28 June 2026, and the projected study completion date is 28 June 2028. Inclusion criteria The patients aged 18–75 years (inclusive), weighing ≥40 kg or with a body mass index (BMI) >18.5, with adequate organ functions, with histologically and/or cytologically confirmed unresectable advanced/refractory HER2-negative or unknown HER2 status with G/GEJ cancer; with at least one measurable lesion as per RECIST (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors) 1.1 ; with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance score of 0 or 1; with a life expectancy of at least 3 months; without prior exposure to anti-cancer treatment. Additionally, patients who had received platinum, paclitaxel or 5-FU as adjuvant treatments and had refractory disease after at least 6 months with grade ≤2 toxicities; anti-VEGFR or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 treatment-naïve patients will also be included. Detailed inclusion criteria are presented in . Exclusion criteria Patients with other malignant tumours, except cured early-stage tumours like basal cell carcinoma of the skin, cervical carcinoma in situ, stage I lung cancer, stage I CRC, etc, which do not affect patient’s life in short term as determined by the investigator; had participated in other clinical trials within <4 weeks; with swallowing difficulties, chronic diarrhoea and intestinal obstruction, which can affect the effectiveness of the oral medication, with a history of immunodeficiency, severe chronic autoimmune diseases or hypersensitivity, bleeding or any bleeding event with grade ≥3 according to the NCI CTCAE V.5.0 within 4 weeks before screening and with known hypersensitivities will be excluded. Detailed exclusion criteria are presented in . Follow-up Safety follow-up will be carried out within 30 days (±7 days) after end-of-treatment (EOT) (or before the start of new anticancer treatment, whichever occurs first) in patients with at least one dose of study treatment. EOT visit during which tumour efficacy assessments indicate

and intestinal obstruction, which can affect the effectiveness of the oral medication, with a history of immunodeficiency, severe chronic autoimmune diseases or hypersensitivity, bleeding or any bleeding event with grade ≥3 according to the NCI CTCAE V.5.0 within 4 weeks before screening and with known hypersensitivities will be excluded. Detailed exclusion criteria are presented in . Follow-up Safety follow-up will be carried out within 30 days (±7 days) after end-of-treatment (EOT) (or before the start of new anticancer treatment, whichever occurs first) in patients with at least one dose of study treatment. EOT visit during which tumour efficacy assessments indicate disease progression and lead to discontinuation of treatment for that patient may serve as safety follow-up. Furthermore, patients will be followed up after 60 days (±7 days) and 90 days (±7 days) after EOT to assess immune-related adverse events and concomitant medications. After patients discontinue study treatment, information on survival and further anticancer treatment will be collected every 3 months (±14 days) after the safety visit or until death or until loss to follow-up or withdrawal of consent or until termination of the study. Outcome measurements The primary endpoints comprise MTD and ORR. MTD is defined as the combination of fruquintinib, sintilimab and CAPEOX after the patient enters the dose escalation phase. If ≤1 patient experiences DLT during the first 21 days of treatment, they will move on to the higher-dose combination group. However, if ≥2 patients do experience DLT, the previous combination group is considered the MTD. If ≤1 patient experienced DLT at the 5 mg dose level, then that dose level was declared the MTD. If ≥2 patients in the first dose cohort experience DLT, 3 additional patients should be enrolled. If ≥2 of these additional patients experience DLT, the chemotherapy dosage should be reduced. ORR is defined as the percentage of patients whose tumours shrink and stay reduced for a certain duration, which includes both CR and partial response (PR). The evaluation of tumour response will be conducted using the RECIST 1.1 criteria categorising it as CR, PR, stable disease or progressive disease based on the measurable tumour lesions observed at baseline. Secondary endpoints include OS, PFS, DCR, duration of response, conversion rate and adverse events and assessment of quality of life (QoL) using European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer QoL questionnaire-Core 30 (EORTC QLQ-C30), EORTC-QLQ-STO (Stomach) 22 and European QoL 5-Dimension 5-Level Health Questionnaire. Molecular biomarkers for predicting therapeutic efficacy will also be explored (refer to for definitions). Statistical analysis The statistical analysis will be conducted after the completion of the study and database lock. The intention-to-treat analysis set will include all the enrolled patients whereas the safety analysis set will include all the patients who received at least one dose of study drug. Further safety analysis will include PD-L1-positive analysis set and TMB-H analysis set. PD-L1-positive analysis set will include all the patients who are PD-L1 positive while the tumour mutational burden (TMB-H) analysis set will include patients with TMB ≥10 mut/Mb. The Kaplan-Meier method will be used to estimate the median mPFS and OS. Descriptive statistics will be used to present the number of cases and percentages, and the 95% CI of the percentages will be also computed. The safety data set will be analysed to evaluate safety and tolerability using descriptive statistics. Adverse events and the results from biochemical and other laboratory test results will be summarised and listed using medical dictionary for regulatory activities terminology. The analysis will include vital signs, physical examinations, electrocardiograms and clinical outcomes (refer to for more details). The patient and public involvement There was no patient or public involvement in the design and conduct of this study. Sample size calculation In the phase three randomised controlled ORIENT-16 study, chemotherapy (XELOX regimen) combined with 1L sintilimab + maintenance therapy had an ORR of 58.2% in all randomised control populations. According to the one arm binomial calculation, if the combination of the treatment drug fruquintinib+sintilimab + CAPEOX regimen can increase the ORR to 75.8%, 2-sided alpha is 0.05, beta is 0.2 and the calculated sample size was calculated to be 57. Considering a 10% dropout rate, 64 patients are ultimately required to be enrolled. Six of the nine patients in the dose escalation phase will be in the non-RP2D dose group and a total of seventy patients are required including the escalation phase. Discussion China is the country with the highest incidence rates of mortality rates of GC globally, with 20% of its population accounting for approximately 50% of global statistics. The impact of disease is severe. In contrast to other Asian countries such as Japan and Korea, nearly 80% of patients with GC in China are diagnosed as stages III or IV. Previously, treatment for advanced GC included 5-FU, platinum, paclitaxel and combinations. However, several studies

nine patients in the dose escalation phase will be in the non-RP2D dose group and a total of seventy patients are required including the escalation phase. Discussion China is the country with the highest incidence rates of mortality rates of GC globally, with 20% of its population accounting for approximately 50% of global statistics. The impact of disease is severe. In contrast to other Asian countries such as Japan and Korea, nearly 80% of patients with GC in China are diagnosed as stages III or IV. Previously, treatment for advanced GC included 5-FU, platinum, paclitaxel and combinations. However, several studies demonstrated that the efficacy had hardly improved. The median OS of 1L treatment was merely 1 year and reducing along with the treatment line. ToGA study reported the patients with HER2-positive GC treated with the addition of trastuzumab achieved a median OS of 13.8 months. However, the prognosis of HER2-negative patients remained unfavourable. The trend persisted until the introduction of PD-1/L1, which has the potential to stimulate the body’s antitumour immune response. Based on the improved outcomes of CheckMate 649, ATTRACTION-4, ORIENT-16, RATIONALE-305 and KENOTE-859 studies, PD-1 blockade in combination with chemotherapy was recommended in NCCN and Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology guidelines for treatment of advanced HER2-negative/unknown GC. The response rate for ICIs combined with chemotherapy as a 1L treatment for HER2-negative/unknown advanced GC ranges from 50% to 60%, which varies based on factors like PD-L1 expression. Further investigation is needed to identify potentially more effective treatment regimens, including surgery options for patients with unresectable diseases. Several studies indicate that small-molecule anti-angiogenic agents used alongside immunotherapy can improve the tumour immune microenvironment, thereby enhancing anti-cancer efficacy. These agents help normalise aberrant blood vessels, improving blood flow, by which the sensitivity to chemotherapy is increased with intravascular drug delivery and the cytotoxicity to tumour cells and/or endothelial cells. Previous studies such as SPACE and TALENT, along with our clinical experience, indicate that the combination of antiangiogenic agents, chemotherapy and PD-1 blockade may lead to improved outcomes for advanced GC with manageable toxicity. Fruquintinib is a highly selective small-molecule inhibitor targeting VEGFR-1, VEGFR-2 and VEGFR-3. In a GC patient-derived xenograft model, the combination of fruquintinib plus chemotherapy significantly enhanced the anti-tumour response without exacerbating the weight loss associated with chemotherapy. A phase 1b/2 study in advanced GC demonstrated that fruquintinib increased paclitaxel exposure by over 30%. Additionally, the phase 3 FRUTIGA study showed that the combination of fruquintinib and paclitaxel was more effective than paclitaxel alone in treating advanced G/GEJ cancers. This provides insights on whether fruquintinib can provide better benefits for patients with HER2-negative GC in 1L. We designed this single-arm, open-label, multicentre phase 1b/2 trial to evaluate the efficacy of fruquintinib in combination with sintilimab and CAPEOX as a 1L treatment for unresectable or metastatic G/GEJ cancer. The trial is aimed at identifying a more effective treatment regimen with manageable toxicity for further clinical practice. Stratification analysis will be conducted based on Lauren subtype, expression of PD-L1 and Claudin 18.2, EBV(Epstein-Barr Virus), MMR and other factors. Next-generation sequencing and immune microenvironment assessments will be performed for biomarker exploration. Further, the QoL will be evaluated through EORTC QLQ-C30 and EQ-5D questionnaires. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the combination of fruquintinib, sintilimab and CAPEOX regimen for its clinical efficacy and safety in treating G/GEJ cancers. However, this study has some limitations. This is an open-label prospective study, without a control group and no randomisation. Furthermore, the single-arm design may result in a treatment bias which could be challenging in distinguishing the individual treatment efficacy of each component in the combination. As this will be initially assessed in Chinese patients which might limit the wide applicability and generalisability of the outcomes. However, this study has some limitations. This is an open-label prospective study, without a control group, and no randomisation. Furthermore, the single-arm design may result in a treatment bias which could be challenging in distinguishing the individual treatment efficacy of each component in the combination. As this will be initially assessed in Chinese patients which might limit the wide applicability and generalisability of the outcomes. Overall, this trial has the potential to enhance 1L treatment options for patients with advanced HER2-negative/unknown G/GEJ cancer. It may facilitate a better understanding of the efficacy and practicality of antiangiogenic agents alongside ICIs and chemotherapy for advanced GC. The exploration of biomarkers could refine the approach to precision medicine. Moreover, this trial has the potential to increase the surgical conversion rate, thereby necessitating a larger-scale RCT in the future. Ethics and dissemination This study will be

Ethics and dissemination This study will be conducted in full compliance with the ICH GCP guidelines, the rules of the Declaration of Helsinki and ICH E2A Guidelines (Clinical Research Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting). The study protocol has received approval from the Henan Cancer Hospital ethical committee (approval No. 2023-237-002). To date, nine other public hospitals have either obtained ethical approval or are undergoing ethical review, while six public hospitals have yet to initiate the process. Participant enrolment commenced on 28 February 2024 and is ongoing, with 38 participants enrolled so far (see for further details). Written informed consent will be obtained from all patients prior to enrolment (see ). For patients who have the mental capacity for informed consent, their consent for participation will be sought and will not be overridden by their family members. For patients who have impaired cognition, informed consent will be sought from their legally acceptable representative. On completion of the analyses, the study findings will be disseminated locally and internationally through manuscript publications in peer-reviewed journals and conference presentations. chunks.content: Introduction Traumatic brain injury (TBI) commonly produces persistent cognitive deficits, including those of attention and executive function. , Corticostriatal interactions are important for efficient cognitive control, and we have previously shown that abnormalities in functional connectivity between the caudate and anterior cingulate cortex are correlated with post-traumatic impairments of executive function. , Caudate activity is modulated by catecholaminergic input into the striatum, hence drugs that modulate striatal dopamine and noradrenaline levels could influence attention and executive function through an effect on corticostriatal interactions. Methylphenidate is a stimulant medication that increases extracellular dopamine and noradrenaline. It is widely used as a treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), in which it can produce marked improvements in attention and executive function. Here we investigate the mechanism of methylphenidate on corticostriatal interactions measured using functional MRI (fMRI). Cognitive impairments are associated with abnormalities of large-scale intrinsic connectivity networks and are frequently observed following TBI. , For example, abnormalities in the default mode network (DMN) and linked intrinsic connectivity networks are associated with impairments in goal-directed cognition. , During externally directed attention, the DMN shows anti-correlated activity with the executive control and salience networks. Change in the extent of this anti-correlation is a mechanism for modulating goal-directed cognition, with greater degrees of anti-correlation being associated with improved executive functioning. The salience network and the corticostriatal systems to which it links are proposed to be important for controlling the balance between intrinsic connectivity networks, , and reduced caudate functional connectivity to the salience network is associated with impairments in executive functioning following TBI. In healthy individuals, methylphenidate can improve selective and sustained attention, , processing speed, , response inhibition, learning rate, , declarative memory, working memory , and choice impulsivity. The neural basis of these effects can be studied using fMRI. For example, in healthy individuals performing response inhibition tasks during fMRI, methylphenidate increases activation bilaterally in the caudate heads, primary motor cortex and right inferior parietal cortex. During successfully inhibited trials, methylphenidate reduces activation in the right inferior frontal gyrus near the anterior insula, while enhancing putamen, dorsomedial frontal cortex and anterior cingulate activation during response inhibition errors. Methylphenidate-induced increases in frontostriatal connectivity are associated with improved performance on a choice impulsivity task, and increased dissociation between the frontoparietal network and the DMN is associated with enhanced working memory. The effect of methylphenidate is therefore context specific and differentially influences distinct functional networks. In fact, following a single dose of methylphenidate, activity is increased in a task-derived ‘high-attention’ network and reduced in a ‘low-attention’ network, compared with unmedicated controls, with the strength of activation in these attentional networks predicting sustained attention. , Taken together, these findings suggest that the cognitive enhancement effects of methylphenidate are achieved through the modulation of functional brain networks and their associated regions. Methylphenidate is used to treat post-traumatic cognitive impairments. The drug produces improvements in attention, information processing speed, executive function, including working memory, , , , and memory. , However, the response to methylphenidate following TBI is variable and greater in patients with reduced striatal dopamine levels. , , Its therapeutic effects in TBI might be mediated through modulation of large-scale network dynamics. For example, methylphenidate can increase subcortical–cortical connectivity between the ventral tegmental area and the posterior cingulate cortex, a key hub of the DMN crucial for attentional regulation, in TBI patients. Furthermore, methylphenidate-induced improvements in reaction time are associated with reduced activity in the left posterior superior parietal cortex and parieto-occipital junction and increased functional motor network connectivity. Methylphenidate also normalizes activity within the right inferior frontal gyrus and its connectivity to parts of the DMN during response inhibition. In another fMRI study, under methylphenidate administration, connectivity abnormalities between cerebellum and inferior parietal cortex, in addition to inferior frontal and subcortical areas, were restored, and working memory deficits in TBI patients were normalized. Overall, the literature suggests that methylphenidate treatment enhances functional connectivity between brain regions involved in attention and executive functioning, which might underlie the observed improvements in cognitive performance in TBI patients. Taken together, these results suggest that further investigation into catecholaminergic modulation of whole-brain network dynamics, and specifically cortical–subcortical interactions, in TBI is warranted. Here, we use fMRI to investigate the modulatory effects of methylphenidate on corticostriatal interactions following moderate–severe TBI. In an experimental medicine add-on study to a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover clinical trial, we focused on the action of methylphenidate on caudate connectivity to test the mechanism of cognitive enhancement from a network neuroscience perspective. We investigate whether methylphenidate strengthens functional connectivity to regions that support externally focused attention and decreases functional connectivity to DMN regions activated when attention is internally directed ( ). We test the following specific hypotheses: (i) caudate functional connectivity to regions involved in executive control will be increased under methylphenidate administration compared with placebo; (ii) methylphenidate

of methylphenidate on corticostriatal interactions following moderate–severe TBI. In an experimental medicine add-on study to a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover clinical trial, we focused on the action of methylphenidate on caudate connectivity to test the mechanism of cognitive enhancement from a network neuroscience perspective. We investigate whether methylphenidate strengthens functional connectivity to regions that support externally focused attention and decreases functional connectivity to DMN regions activated when attention is internally directed ( ). We test the following specific hypotheses: (i) caudate functional connectivity to regions involved in executive control will be increased under methylphenidate administration compared with placebo; (ii) methylphenidate will also influence caudate functional connectivity with the DMN; (iii) post-traumatic hyperconnectivity within the DMN will be reduced following methylphenidate administration; (iv) normalization of caudate functional connectivity will be associated with improved post-traumatic cognitive function; and (v) the effects of methylphenidate on caudate functional connectivity will be influenced by dopamine levels within the caudate, measured with 123 I-Ioflupane single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) dopamine transporter (DAT) scanning. Materials and methods Study population Forty-three patients following a moderate–severe TBI ≥6 months previously were recruited from neurology clinics. Fifteen patients were excluded from the functional imaging analyses based on stringent criteria for assessing the possible impact of movement during the resting-state scan (see for demographics of all 43 patients, including details on who was excluded). Hence, the data presented here included 28 patients with neuropsychological and functional imaging analysis (four females, mean age 40.9 ± 12.7 years, range 20–65 years). Mean time since injury was 89.2 ± 38 months (range 6–366 months; please see De Simoni et al . and Jenkins et al . for details on the larger cohort of patients). TBI severity was assessed according to the Mayo classification. All patients were identified as having persistent cognitive problems by the patient themselves, treating clinician or caregiver. Inclusion criteria required the patient to be aged 20–65 years, with no significant premorbid psychiatric or neurological history, alcohol or substance misuse, or significant additional previous TBI. Exclusion criteria included contraindication to MRI and a positive urine drug screen. Written, informed consent was obtained from all patients in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by the West London & GTAC Research Ethics Committee (14/LO/0067). Study design The dataset included in this paper is derived from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover trial, aspects of which have been published previously. , , All participants enrolled in the trial had a baseline 123 I-ioflupane single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) DAT scan, MRI and neuropsychological assessment. After baseline assessment, the TBI patients were randomized using a block design (block size four) into one of two treatment groups: 2 weeks of methylphenidate with crossover to 2 weeks of placebo, or vice versa ( ). The crossover design allowed for within-subject control, thereby reducing the variance in outcome measures. Patients received either placebo or 0.3 mg/kg rounded to the nearest 5 mg (maximum 25 mg) of methylphenidate, twice daily (morning, midday). This dose has been used in previous research studies investigating the effects of methylphenidate in TBI patients and is within the dosage range commonly prescribed in clinical settings. Study drugs were prepared as 5 mg tablets of methylphenidate and matching placebo (Clinical Trials Manufacturing and Supplies Department, Royal Free London NHS Trust). Carryover effects of methylphenidate were considered to be minimal, because it is a short-acting stimulant with a pharmacokinetic half-life of 2–3 h. Only data in TBI patients collected during the crossover part of the trial are included in this paper. Neuropsychological assessment A standardized neuropsychological battery was used to assess cognitive function, including tests previously shown to be sensitive to TBI-related deficits. Measures of pre-morbid IQ and differences in neuropsychological performance between TBI patients and healthy controls have been reported previously by De Simoni et al . Cognitive impairments were seen primarily in information processing speed and executive function, and abnormalities in caudate connectivity were associated with these impairments. Here, we therefore focus on these measures to assess how this relationship might be altered under methylphenidate administration. To this end, the trail making test (TMT) and Delis–Kaplan executive function system (D-KEFS) colour–word interference (Stroop) test were used to assess information processing speed and executive function, including inhibition and task switching. Statistical analysis of neuropsychological data Shapiro–Wilk tests revealed that data were non-normally distributed. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to assess within-group differences between placebo and methylphenidate conditions. Neuroimaging Imaging acquisition MRI data were acquired using a 3 T Siemens Magnetom Verio Syngo using a 32-channel head coil. Standard clinical MR imaging was collected, including a T 2 -weighted inversion recovery turbo spin echo (IR-TSE) (30 transverse slices 4 mm thick, repetition time (TR) = 9000 ms, echo time (TE) = 95 ms, flip angle = 130°, matrix size = 256 × 256,

executive function, including inhibition and task switching. Statistical analysis of neuropsychological data Shapiro–Wilk tests revealed that data were non-normally distributed. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to assess within-group differences between placebo and methylphenidate conditions. Neuroimaging Imaging acquisition MRI data were acquired using a 3 T Siemens Magnetom Verio Syngo using a 32-channel head coil. Standard clinical MR imaging was collected, including a T 2 -weighted inversion recovery turbo spin echo (IR-TSE) (30 transverse slices 4 mm thick, repetition time (TR) = 9000 ms, echo time (TE) = 95 ms, flip angle = 130°, matrix size = 256 × 256, field of view = 22 cm × 22 cm) and T 2 *-susceptibility-weighted (SWI) scans (128 transverse slices 1281.2 mm thick, TR = 28 ms, TE = 20 ms, flip angle = 15°, in-plane resolution = 0.6 mm × 0.5 mm, matrix size = 448 × 448, field of view = 23 cm × 23 cm) to assess microbleeds. Functional T 2 *-weighted eyes-closed resting-state (r)fMRI data were collected using gradient echo-planar imaging. A total of 300 volumes of 35 slices (3 mm thickness, no interslice gap) were acquired in an interleaved manner during a 10-min scan (TE = 30 ms, TR = 2000ms, flip angle = 80°, in-plane resolution = 3 mm × 3 mm, matrix size = 64 × 64, field of view = 19.2 cm × 19.2 cm). Structural MRI included a T 1 -weighted high-resolution magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo (MPRAGE, 160 transverse slices 1 mm thick, TR = 2300 ms, TE = 2.98 ms, flip angle = 9°, in-plane resolution = 1 mm × 1 mm, matrix size = 256 × 256, field of view = 25.6 cm × 25.6 cm). <sup>123</sup>I-Ioflupane SPECT Prior to placebo or methylphenidate administration, all TBI patients had a 123 I-ioflupane SPECT DAT scan with standard acquisition parameters. A bolus intravenous injection of 123 I-ioflupane was administered (mean activity 185 MBq; GE Healthcare Ltd). A dual-headed gamma camera (Symbia T16, Siemens Healthcare) was used to acquire all SPECT images at 180 min post-injection with LEHR collimators, 1.45 zoom, 128 × 128 matrix, 128 projections, and 30 s per projection. Reconstructed SPECT images were registered into Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space using a three-step procedure. First, reconstructed SPECT images were co-registered with their native T 1 structural MRI image using rigid transformation. Second, T 1 images underwent tissue segmentation using SPM12 to produce grey and white matter images. These templates were then warped to create an average group template using a diffeomorphic non-linear registration (DARTEL). Finally, transformation parameters obtained from registering this group template to MNI space were then applied to the SPECT images to produce MNI space images (see Jenkins et al . for full details; ). Imaging analysis Preprocessing The first two volumes of the resting-state fMRI (rfMRI) were removed to account for the T 1 equilibrium effect. Image pre-processing involved a rigid-body realignment to correct for motion between volumes, temporal frequency filtering using a high-pass filter (100 s), followed by spatial smoothing using a 6 mm full-width at half-maximum kernel. Functional images were registered into standard MNI space using parameters defined by registering the individual high-resolution T 1 images to the MNI standard template, performed using boundary-based registration (BBR). Pre-processed rfMRI data were subjected to whole-brain independent components analysis (ICA) decomposition to identify spatially independent temporal components. There are several advantages to using an ICA-based approach for data denoising over ‘scrubbing’ techniques, in which individual volumes are removed. These include more comprehensive noise removal (including physiological and scanner-induced artefacts rather than primarily addressing motion), preservation of temporal continuity in the data, and avoidance of loss of temporal degrees of freedom owing to a reduction in the number of available volumes. Components considered to be artefact were removed using FSL’s FIX, previously trained on an independent dataset of 20 healthy controls. The accuracy of FIX classification was also assessed manually. All components were inspected visually using spatial maps, time series and power spectra, and those considered to be noise as per published guidance were removed. Frame-wise displacement (FD), a measure of how much the head position changes from one frame to the next, was obtained for each volume of raw rfMRI data using the FSL motion outliers tool. , Motion was considered excessive if there was an FD of >0.5 mm in >15% of volumes and/or an FD of >3 mm (size of one voxel) across any of the volumes. A subset of 15 patients were excluded from the imaging analysis owing to excessive motion. Defining striatal subdivisions and corresponding corticostriatal networks in healthy controls A set of striatal subdivisions and corresponding corticostriatal functional connectivity networks were defined in a previous publication using a large independent dataset with high spatial and temporal resolution. This independent dataset included rfMRI data obtained

rfMRI data using the FSL motion outliers tool. , Motion was considered excessive if there was an FD of >0.5 mm in >15% of volumes and/or an FD of >3 mm (size of one voxel) across any of the volumes. A subset of 15 patients were excluded from the imaging analysis owing to excessive motion. Defining striatal subdivisions and corresponding corticostriatal networks in healthy controls A set of striatal subdivisions and corresponding corticostriatal functional connectivity networks were defined in a previous publication using a large independent dataset with high spatial and temporal resolution. This independent dataset included rfMRI data obtained from 100 healthy controls from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). This approach provided a robust parcellation of the caudate, enabling a data-driven exploration of the spatially distinct subdivisions and their functional connectivity patterns with cortical areas. The resulting subdivisions and networks are used in this paper to examine the effect of methylphenidate on corticostriatal connectivity following TBI ( ). A combined masked (m)ICA and dual-regression approach was used to identify corticostriatal functional connectivity networks within the HCP data. mICA was performed using a Harvard atlas-defined striatal mask and resulted in 12 spatially independent striatal subdivisions, including four caudate (located in anterior and posterior parts of the right and left caudate) and eight putamen subdivisions. None in the nucleus accumbens were found. Twelve corresponding dual regression analyses were then used to identify whole-brain corticostriatal connectivity. Caudate connectivity in traumatic brain injury patients Striatal subdivisions and corresponding whole-brain networks defined in the HCP dataset were then used to examine differences in corticostriatal connectivity during the baseline assessment of TBI patients and healthy controls recruited into the clinical study. Alterations in functional connectivity associated with TBI were found only within cortico-caudate networks. These caudate networks included similar areas, including the anterior cingulate and paracingulate cortices, alongside superior and inferior frontal cortices, supramarginal cortex, thalamus, insula and cerebellum. TBI-associated reductions in connectivity within these networks were mainly evident in the anterior cingulate cortex and supramarginal gyrus. Defining differences in corticostriatal connectivity between methylphenidate and placebo conditions For this analysis, we evaluated a subset of the TBI patients who underwent baseline assessments in the main clinical trial. Specifically, we investigated the effects of methylphenidate on functional connectivity within the previously defined caudate networks that were shown to have abnormal functional connectivity in TBI. Methylphenidate-induced modulation of caudate-to-DMN connectivity and within-DMN connectivity was also examined to address hypotheses outlined in the Introduction. The DMN network used in analyses was defined by Smith et al . Dopamine transporter levels DAT levels in the right anterior caudate were calculated from the 123 I-ioflupane SPECT DAT scans as described by Jenkins et al . Age was regressed from caudate DAT values. Statistical analysis of imaging data Nine dual regression analyses were conducted to assess differences in connectivity between placebo and methylphenidate conditions in TBI patients ( ). Four dual regressions assessed caudate connectivity to the whole-brain networks identified within the HCP cohort. An additional four dual regressions were performed to examine caudate-to-DMN connectivity. For each dual regression, a different caudate subdivision was used to perform the analysis; each was constrained to voxels within the relevant network. The final dual regression examined within-DMN connectivity. Between-group effects were assessed using non-parametric permutation testing, thresholded using threshold-free cluster enhancement and family-wise error corrected for multiple comparisons at P < 0.05. To investigate the effect that methylphenidate has on the relationship between corticostriatal connectivity and cognition, linear mixed-effects models were used. Drug condition (methylphenidate or placebo) and cognitive performance were defined as within-subject fixed effects, and subject was defined as a random effect to model variability in subjects’ intercepts. To investigate the relationship between functional connectivity and baseline dopaminergic abnormalities, Spearman’s rank correlations were performed separately for the placebo and methylphenidate groups. Control analysis An additional ‘control’ functional connectivity analysis was performed within the executive control network to assess the specificity of methylphenidate-associated changes to corticostriatal connectivity. Functional connectivity within the executive control network, defined from functional connectivity analysis of rfMRI data, was assessed and compared between methylphenidate and placebo conditions. Clinical variables Heart rate was obtained outside of the scanner as part of the routine physical examination at each visit. Owing to technical difficulties, physiological data from six participants were not recorded. The analysis of heart rate was thus performed on the remaining 22 participants. Lesion probability maps ( ) were produced to provide a description of the pattern of focal cortical damage sustained within the cohort. Brain areas with focal lesions were masked using semi-automatic segmentation methods based upon an algorithm for geodesic image segmentation as described by Criminisi et al . and implemented in IMSEG v.1.8. Fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T 1 -weighted images were co-registered, and lesion maps were drawn as overlays on the T 1 -weighted

technical difficulties, physiological data from six participants were not recorded. The analysis of heart rate was thus performed on the remaining 22 participants. Lesion probability maps ( ) were produced to provide a description of the pattern of focal cortical damage sustained within the cohort. Brain areas with focal lesions were masked using semi-automatic segmentation methods based upon an algorithm for geodesic image segmentation as described by Criminisi et al . and implemented in IMSEG v.1.8. Fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T 1 -weighted images were co-registered, and lesion maps were drawn as overlays on the T 1 -weighted images guided by overlapping FLAIR images. The additional use of FLAIR images was to improve the visual contrast of lesions compared with T 1 -weighted images alone and thus promote greater accuracy when creating masks of lesioned voxels (see ). Results Methylphenidate modulates corticostriatal functional connectivity We investigated whether methylphenidate modulates the functional connectivity from the caudate to cortical networks involved in cognitive control. In previous work, we defined a network of cortical regions showing strong functional connectivity to the caudate. These connected networks included the anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri, in addition to the thalamus, insula, cerebellum, supramarginal gyrus, superior and inferior frontal gyri. Post-traumatic abnormalities in cortico-caudate connectivity correlated with post-traumatic impairments in processing speed and executive function. Hence, we investigated whether methylphenidate modulated functional connectivity between each of the caudate subdivisions and their previously defined connected networks, as shown in . All resulting statistical maps were thresholded at P < 0.05. Methylphenidate increased corticostriatal connectivity in TBI when compared with placebo ( ). Increases in functional connectivity were evident for three of the four caudate subdivisions. Anterior and posterior subdivisions of the right caudate showed a similar increase in functional connectivity to the anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri, extending into the superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri. In addition, the right posterior subdivision showed increases in functional connectivity to regions within the fronto-orbital, fronto-opercular and insular cortices ( ). In contrast, the left anterior caudate subdivision showed increases in functional connectivity to the posterior cingulate and precuneus, extending into the lingual gyrus and calcarine cortices ( ). There was no alteration in functional connectivity from the left posterior caudate subdivision. Next, we investigated whether methylphenidate modulated caudate connectivity with the DMN, which typically shows anti-correlated activity during attentionally demanding tasks with the cortico-caudate network defined directly from caudate functional connectivity. Methylphenidate decreased caudate–DMN connectivity, with significant decreases evident across all four caudate subdivisions ( ). Anterior right and left caudate subdivisions showed decreases in functional connectivity to all cortical brain regions commonly associated with the DMN, including the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, precuneus and lateral inferior parietal lobes. The posterior left caudate showed a similar pattern of change, although decreases within the ventromedial regions were less extensive. Likewise, the posterior right caudate subdivision decreases in functional connectivity were restricted to posterior regions of the DMN, including the posterior cingulate and precuneus ( ). Next, we investigated whether methylphenidate modulated functional connectivity within the DMN and within the executive control network, which includes many of the regions within the corticostriatal functional connectivity maps previously studied. Hyperconnectivity of the DMN is seen chronically after TBI, and we show in this study that methylphenidate decreases DMN connectivity in TBI ( ). Decreases were evident in all cortical regions associated with the DMN, including the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, precuneus and lateral inferior parietal lobes. Decreases in functional connectivity within posterior regions of the DMN appear more extensive than in anterior regions ( ). Methylphenidate did not produce any changes of functional connectivity within the executive control network. Methylphenidate modulates the relationship between functional connectivity and cognition Next, we investigated how the relationship between caudate functional connectivity and cognitive performance was influenced by methylphenidate. We focused this analysis on measures of processing speed and executive function that had previously been shown to be correlated with the functional connectivity of the anterior caudate subdivisions. At baseline, TBI patients in the larger clinical trial cohort were significantly impaired in measures of executive function and processing speed compared with healthy controls. The 28 patients assessed in this study also showed significant impairments in processing speed and executive function ( ). Under the influence of methylphenidate, patients showed improvements in executive function. Specifically, the Stroop inhibition-switching cost was significantly reduced in the methylphenidate condition compared with placebo [methylphenidate = 61.81 s, standard deviation (SD) 14.58 s; placebo = 66.33 s, SD 16.93 s; V = 103.5, P = 0.039, Cohen’s d = −0.28]. There was also a trend towards a reduction in the Stroop inhibition switching versus baseline contrast (methylphenidate = 37.74 s, SD = 13.40 s; placebo = 33.76 seconds, SD = 11.66 s; V = 110, P = 0.059, Cohen’s d

in processing speed and executive function ( ). Under the influence of methylphenidate, patients showed improvements in executive function. Specifically, the Stroop inhibition-switching cost was significantly reduced in the methylphenidate condition compared with placebo [methylphenidate = 61.81 s, standard deviation (SD) 14.58 s; placebo = 66.33 s, SD 16.93 s; V = 103.5, P = 0.039, Cohen’s d = −0.28]. There was also a trend towards a reduction in the Stroop inhibition switching versus baseline contrast (methylphenidate = 37.74 s, SD = 13.40 s; placebo = 33.76 seconds, SD = 11.66 s; V = 110, P = 0.059, Cohen’s d = −0.31). There was no improvement in processing speed under the influence of methylphenidate (trail making B, placebo = 57.46 s, SD = 27.99 s; methylphenidate = 62.7 s, SD = 34.22 s; V = 224, P = 0.224, Cohen’s d = 0.167). Results of all components of the trail making test and the Stroop task are reported in . Methylphenidate significantly altered the relationship of anterior caudate functional connectivity to measures of information processing and executive function ( ). For trail making B in the placebo condition, decreasing caudate connectivity was associated with increasing processing speed, which was not seen under the influence of methylphenidate. This is reflected in the significant effect of drug on the relationship between both right and left anterior caudate functional connectivity with task performance [right: F (49) = 12.01, P = 0.001; left: F (49) = 11.55, P = 0.001] and a significant drug condition × processing speed interaction [right: F (30.3) = 5.45, P = 0.026; left: F (48) = 5.41, P = 0.024]. In the Stroop inhibition switch time compared with baseline contrast, there was a significant effect of executive processing speed on left anterior caudate functional connectivity [ F (51) = 10.32, P = 0.002]. There was a significant effect of drug condition on right and left anterior caudate functional connectivity [right: F (26.92) = 11.84, P = 0.002; left: F (51) = 9.95, P = 0.002]. As caudate connectivity decreases, executive dysfunction increases, whereas under methylphenidate administration slight increases in functional connectivity occur with increased executive dysfunction, as reflected in the significant interaction between drug and executive functioning [right: F (30.14) =5.01, P = 0.033; left: F (50) = 7.10, P = 0.010]. Dopamine transporter binding ratios are correlated with caudate functional connectivity on methylphenidate We have previously shown that the cognitive effects of methylphenidate following TBI are influenced by dopaminergic abnormalities measures by 123 I-ioflupane SPECT. Around one-third of patients showed a reduction in striatal dopamine following moderate–severe TBI, but there are large variations in dopamine transporter levels measured using 123 I-ioflupane SPECT ( ). We assessed whether pretreatment DAT levels affected the influence of methylphenidate on the relationship between anterior right caudate DAT and anterior right caudate functional connectivity. During methylphenidate administration, anterior right caudate 123 I-ioflupane SPECT was positively correlated with the functional connectivity of the region ( R = 0.49, P = 0.01; ). A similar correlation measured during placebo administration was not significant ( R = 0.22, P = 0.26). Assessment of motion and heart rate effects We carefully investigated the potential effects of lesions, motion and non-neural physiological artefacts on FC. Data were denoised to remove motion and artefacts relating to physiological noise (for example, heart rate and respiration). Focal lesions were present in 21 patients. Descriptions of clinical imaging findings for all TBI patients can be found in . shows the spatial distribution of lesions across all TBI patients, illustrating a minimal overlap of lesions and brain regions assessed with functional connectivity analyses. Fifteen patients exceeded criteria for excessive motion and were thus excluded from further imaging analysis ( ). Motion was minimal across the remaining 28 participants [<0.33 mm in mean frame-wise displacement (FD)]. Following these exclusions, differences in motion remained evident between methylphenidate and placebo conditions. Significant differences in FD of the raw data were found between treatment conditions ( V = 16, P < 0.001), with TBI patients demonstrating a median of 0.10 and 0.16 mm during the administration of methylphenidate and placebo, respectively. There was no significant relationship between movement and corticostriatal functional connectivity. For the DMN functional connectivity results, these were unrelated to measures taken during methylphenidate administration, but functional connectivity between the right anterior caudate and the DMN ( P < 0.01) and within-DMN connectivity ( P < 0.01) were correlated with movement during placebo administration (see ‘Results’ section). Heart rate was significantly higher during methylphenidate (median heart rate = 78.7 beats/min) administration compared with placebo (median heart rate = 62.32 beats/min; V = 189, P = 0.001). There were no significant relationships between heart rate and functional connectivity in either treatment condition (see ‘Results’ section). results, these were unrelated to measures taken during methylphenidate administration, but functional connectivity between the right anterior caudate and the DMN ( P < 0.01) and within-DMN connectivity ( P < 0.01) were correlated with movement during placebo administration (see ‘Results’ section). Heart rate was significantly higher during methylphenidate (median heart rate = 78.7 beats/min) administration compared with placebo (median heart rate = 62.32 beats/min; V = 189, P = 0.001). There were no significant relationships between heart rate and functional connectivity in either treatment condition (see ‘Results’ section). Discussion We have previously demonstrated reductions in caudate functional connectivity following TBI, particularly with regions involved in executive control, such as the anterior cingulate cortex and insula cortices. Here, we show that the catecholaminergic drug methylphenidate modifies caudate functional connectivity by increasing connectivity to frontal regions, in addition to decreasing connectivity within the DMN, which typically shows abnormally high functional connectivity after TBI. The directions of the effects produced by methylphenidate are consistent with patterns of network connectivity demonstrated by healthy controls in the study by De Simoni et al ., suggesting that the drug is inducing a shift towards more normative brain network dynamics. Increased caudate functional connectivity to frontal regions, including the anterior cingulate, was associated with an improvement in executive function, which was impaired in the group of TBI patients we studied. The results suggest that the beneficial effect of methylphenidate on goal-directed attention and executive function might result from changing the balance of cortical–subcortical network activity towards regions involved in externally directed attention and away from the DMN. Whole-brain network dynamics that underpin cognitive function are under the control of the catecholaminergic systems, which are susceptible to injury following TBI. Cognitive impairment after TBI is associated with reduced striatal dopamine, which, along with noradrenaline, influences the activity and connectivity of intrinsic connectivity networks. , For example, administration of a noradrenergic antagonist reduces connectivity within the salience network, and polymorphisms of the DAT gene ( DAT1 ) influence corticostriatal connectivity. Elevated dopamine signalling, owing to decreased DAT expression, strengthens connectivity between the caudate and anterior cingulate, insula and prefrontal regions, enhancing executive function. L- DOPA, a precursor to dopamine, reduces connectivity within the DMN and its interactions with the caudate. Conversely, decreased dopaminergic signalling is associated with increased between-network connectivity. This relationship between endogenous dopaminergic activity and functional connectivity is directly shown in experimental work conducted by Birn et al. , in which simultaneous PET and fMRI demonstrated that changes in striatal dopamine influence subcortical–cortical functional connectivity in rhesus monkeys. Increasing levels of extracellular dopamine, induced by oral administration of methylphenidate, were associated with increased connectivity of the head of the caudate to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and precuneus —regions involved in attentional control networks. Hence, catecholaminergic effects on striatal functional connectivity provide a mechanism through which methylphenidate exerts influence over cognitive function. Our results are in keeping with the hypothesis that methylphenidate changes the balance of activity within large-scale brain networks involved in cognitive control. During externally directed attention, frontal networks governing cognitive control and the DMN show anti-correlated activity, which increases with executive control. The ability to switch between distinct functional connectivity configurations is important for cognitive control, , and the anterior insula appears important for facilitating this adaptive switching between brain connectivity states. , , Following TBI, connectivity between caudate and corticostriatal networks, including insular cortex, is reduced, and this is associated with executive function impairments. Given that the anterior insula forms part of the network of frontal brain regions where functional connectivity is modulated by methylphenidate, this interaction might be important in supporting efficient switching of attentional control. Changing caudate functional connectivity potentially provides a general control mechanism for the adaptive control of goal-directed and flexible behaviours. , In other contexts, changes in structural and functional connectivity within corticostriatal pathways influence executive function, , and abnormal corticostriatal functional connectivity is associated with cognitive impairments across a range of neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases. , , After TBI, reduced anterior caudate functional connectivity is associated with impairments in processing speed and executive function. In addition, DMN activity is strongly linked to cognitive performance, with load-dependent reductions in DMN activity seen during attentionally demanding tasks and abnormal DMN activity observed in a range of disorders characterized by impairments of attention and executive function, including TBI and ADHD. , Following TBI, patients demonstrate abnormal patterns of activity and functional connectivity within the DMN, , , , and abnormal communication between DMN and the salience network is associated with impaired cognitive control. , In ADHD, the DMN exhibits hyperconnectivity to attentional control networks, and the ability to sustain suppression of the DMN to facilitate outwardly focused attention is reduced. Methylphenidate is widely used to treat ADHD and, consistent with the results presented here, has been proposed to improve

abnormal DMN activity observed in a range of disorders characterized by impairments of attention and executive function, including TBI and ADHD. , Following TBI, patients demonstrate abnormal patterns of activity and functional connectivity within the DMN, , , , and abnormal communication between DMN and the salience network is associated with impaired cognitive control. , In ADHD, the DMN exhibits hyperconnectivity to attentional control networks, and the ability to sustain suppression of the DMN to facilitate outwardly focused attention is reduced. Methylphenidate is widely used to treat ADHD and, consistent with the results presented here, has been proposed to improve cognition in ADHD by promoting balance of the intrinsic connectivity networks required for cognitive control, including facilitating the normalization of DMN activation. For example, improvements in sustained attention in children with ADHD are associated with enhanced spontaneous activity in the salience network and DMN, and abnormal dynamic interactions between the salience network, fronto-parietal network (FPN) and DMN can be remediated with methylphenidate, improving symptoms. Our results are consistent with existing literature showing that methylphenidate induced changes in brain activity are associated with enhanced cognitive function following TBI; for example: (i) improvements on a visual attention task after methylphenidate were associated with reductions in parietal activity ; (ii) improvements in response inhibition were associated with a normalization of right inferior frontal gyrus activity and connectivity to parts of the DMN ; and (iii) improved working memory function was associated with connectivity changes in cerebellar, parietal, frontal and subcortical regions. Our findings complement and extend recent work by Peattie et al ., which demonstrated that methylphenidate can ameliorate executive function deficits in chronic TBI patients by normalizing brain activity and enhancing functional connectivity within task-relevant networks. Specifically, they reported that methylphenidate increased activity and connectivity in regions such as the inferior frontal gyri, insula, striatum and cerebellum, which was correlated with improved performance on the Tower of London task. Our results provide further insights into the neural mechanisms underlying the cognitive benefits of methylphenidate in TBI by specifically examining its modulatory effects on corticostriatal interactions. As reported in De Simoni et al ., TBI patients in the clinical trial cohort exhibited processing speed and executive function deficits compared with healthy controls at baseline, and these were associated with abnormal caudate connectivity. In the present study, we did not show any improvements in processing speed under methylphenidate administration, and only modest improvements in executive function. The present analyses were designed to test specifically whether these cognitive functions, which we previously showed are associated with caudate connectivity, could be improved with methylphenidate, and whether the relationship with functional connectivity changes under its influence. The P -values reported for the tests of improvement in processing speed and executive function on drug are therefore not corrected for multiple comparisons, because we were testing a very specific hypothesis grounded in our prior research. The present results did show significant interactions between drug conditions in the relationship between cognition and caudate connectivity. These results suggest that cognitive effects of methylphenidate might be more pronounced in individuals with pre-existing functional connectivity abnormalities within the affected networks. For example, in those with poor functional connectivity at baseline, methylphenidate might normalize this and produce a cognitive benefit, but in those with intact baseline connectivity patterns, methylphenidate might not have been beneficial, and the modulatory effects of methylphenidate on these networks might not have translated into measurable cognitive improvements at the group level. We also investigated the influence of dopaminergic state on the response to methylphenidate. One-third of moderate–severe TBI patients have abnormal striatal dopamine transporter binding, and the therapeutic efficacy in terms of cognitive enhancement is dependent on the pretreatment DAT levels of an individual. We have previously shown that TBI patients with low 123 I-ioflupane binding (a hypodopaminergic state) demonstrate improvements in information processing speed under the influence of methylphenidate, whereas those with normal or high binding do not. The lack of cognitive enhancement in processing speed in the present results is likely to relate to the inverted U-shaped relationship proposed by Jenkins et al ., whereby those with abnormally low DAT at baseline might reap benefit from methylphenidate, but if DAT is already optimum, the drug will not have an enhancement effect. Here we extend these observations to show that DAT levels in the right anterior caudate are correlated with the functional connectivity of this region under the influence of methylphenidate but not placebo. This is consistent with previous work showing that the main methylphenidate-related changes in resting-state functional connectivity are influenced by the distribution of DAT across the brain. These findings suggest that individual differences in baseline DAT levels in the anterior right caudate might be modulating the effects of methylphenidate on the functional connectivity of this region. Specifically, higher pretreatment DAT levels were associated with greater methylphenidate-induced

an enhancement effect. Here we extend these observations to show that DAT levels in the right anterior caudate are correlated with the functional connectivity of this region under the influence of methylphenidate but not placebo. This is consistent with previous work showing that the main methylphenidate-related changes in resting-state functional connectivity are influenced by the distribution of DAT across the brain. These findings suggest that individual differences in baseline DAT levels in the anterior right caudate might be modulating the effects of methylphenidate on the functional connectivity of this region. Specifically, higher pretreatment DAT levels were associated with greater methylphenidate-induced increases in functional connectivity between the anterior right caudate and other brain areas. There are a number of limitations to be considered. One important consideration is whether movement might have biased our results. We excluded a relatively large number of people because of significant levels of movement, but small amounts of motion remained that were different between groups. To account for this, we took several steps to ensure that physiological motion artefact did not contribute to functional connectivity estimates, including individual independent components analysis of the data for each subject to eliminate components that consist largely of motion. Although there was a significant difference in head motion between treatment conditions, framewise displacement (calculated in the raw data) did not show a significant relationship with functional connectivity estimates with the caudate networks for either methylphenidate or placebo conditions ( , ‘Results’ section). Although head motion was associated with caudate–DMN and within-DMN connectivity during placebo, this relationship was not observed under methylphenidate administration. Therefore, we do not consider head motion a confounding factor in interpreting our results on modulation by methylphenidate of caudate functional connectivity patterns. Likewise, we reported an increase in heart rate under methylphenidate administration, which is expected. , Heart rate can influence functional connectivity estimates, with spontaneous changes in heart rate or breathing patterns inflating whole-brain connectivity estimates. The results we have presented here show both increases and decreases in functional connectivity under the influence of methylphenidate and thus are not likely to be influenced by the changes in heart rate during treatment. Furthermore, there are no significant relationships between functional connectivity and heart rate in either group for any of the results presented here. Finally, an inherent characteristic of a moderate–severe TBI population is the presence of focal lesions ( ). Voxels within lesions were not excluded from the analysis because: (i) this would result in significant data loss owing to the heterogeneity of lesion distribution across participants; and (ii) the cohort remains the same across both treatment conditions and the within-subject study design is controlling for any individual differences in focal lesion distribution. Furthermore, the majority of lesioned voxels across the cohort are remote from the brain regions where we observe the significant effects of methylphenidate on functional connectivity. Conclusion In summary, methylphenidate administration modulates functional connectivity of corticostriatal networks and the DMN to normalize connectivity underpinning cognitive function within and between large-scale brain networks following TBI. Our results demonstrate that the relationship between functional connectivity and cognition is modulated under catecholaminergic intervention. Taken together, we provide evidence that the fine-tuning of large-scale brain networks is a likely mechanism through which pharmacological intervention with methylphenidate achieves cognitive enhancement following traumatic brain injury.
